questions.q: What do RPO and RTO measure, per this lesson?
options: RPO measures downtime; RTO measures data loss
Both measure the exact same thing and are interchangeable
RPO and RTO are licensing terms, not availability metrics
RPO measures tolerable data loss in time; RTO measures tolerable downtime before service is restored
questions.explain: RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is about how much data loss is acceptable; RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is about how long the system can be down.

questions.q: What is a Basic Availability Group, and which edition provides it?
options: A free trial version of AG available in any edition for 30 days
Standard Edition's limited AG: one primary, one secondary, a single database, and no readable secondary
Enterprise Edition's full-featured AG with up to 8 replicas
A feature available only on FCI, not Availability Groups
questions.explain: Basic Availability Groups are a Standard Edition feature: a single primary and secondary, one database per AG, and no readable secondary.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say checking SQL Server edition should happen before designing an HA solution, not as an afterthought?
options: Because Standard Edition doesn't support Availability Groups at all
Because edition has no real effect on which HA technologies are available
Because a design that assumes Enterprise-only features (like multiple readable secondaries) simply won't run on Standard Edition
Because edition only affects backup compression, not HA
questions.explain: Edition determines which AG and FCI features are actually available — designing around Enterprise features first and discovering a Standard Edition license later wastes the design work.

questions.q: Per the worked example, why would an Availability Group with synchronous commit and automatic failover be chosen for a finance database needing zero data loss and a sub-30-second RTO?
options: Because log shipping meets both requirements more cheaply
Because synchronous commit guarantees zero data loss and automatic failover mode meets the fast RTO requirement
Because FCI is always faster than AG for any RTO requirement
Because Standard Edition is sufficient for this scenario
questions.explain: Zero data loss requires synchronous commit specifically, and a sub-30-second RTO requires automatic failover — both point to a synchronous AG configuration with Enterprise licensing.

questions.q: A department wants a 10-second RTO and zero data loss, but is only licensed for SQL Server Standard Edition. What does this lesson's framework say has to change first?
options: Log shipping alone can meet a 10-second RTO
The licensing needs to move to Enterprise Edition (or the RPO/RTO targets need to be relaxed), since Standard's Basic AG and 2-node FCI limits don't support this level of protection at scale
The database should be moved to SIMPLE recovery model
Nothing — Standard Edition already fully supports this scenario
questions.explain: Standard Edition's Basic AG and limited FCI options constrain what's achievable; hitting an aggressive RPO/RTO combination like this typically requires Enterprise Edition licensing, or the targets need to be renegotiated.
